_comment: Facts that are not in a machine-readable evaluation output. Every entry names its source so it can be re-checked. Do not edit a number without re-measuring it.

tests.source: Final local `pytest -q -rs` run (Ollama reachable, so live-LLM tests ran); per-file counts from `pytest --collect-only`.

dataset.source: Counted directly in the Docker PostgreSQL database (crimes, documents, document_chunks).

notes: The same old configuration scored 5, 8, 6 and 7 across four runs; the shipped configuration scored 10, 9, 8, 6 and 8 across five. A 10/10 and a 5/10 are both ordinary draws from a non-deterministic 3B model, so comparing one run with one run proves nothing.
The correctness prompt alone moved the mean by +0.67 questions (n=3 per arm) — smaller than the spread inside any single arm.

Adding bounded repair made no difference to the mean (7.67 vs 7.67). Across those runs 9 repairs were attempted and 3 executed successfully (n=9: too few to generalize). In the final full evaluation, reported separately because it is a different run, 3 queries were repaired and 2 then executed.

Executing is not the same as being right. Reviewing the actual results of one run by hand, 4 of 10 queries that executed returned wrong answers — for example a filter on an invented value that returned all zeros. There is no automated semantic-correctness metric yet.
Safety did not change: malicious prompts were blocked 7/7 in every run of the shipped configuration, and none was ever executed.
The ablation runs predate the literal-% executor fix, so they were not re-run for it.
